title: Unilateral Facial Pain (Trigeminal Neuralgia and its Red-Flag Mimics)
patient_instructions: You are a 58-year-old presenting with pain on the RIGHT side of your face. If asked to describe it: it comes as sudden, very sharp, electric-shock-like stabs lasting a second or so, always on the same right side, triggered by touching your face, chewing, talking, brushing your teeth or a gust of wind. Between attacks you feel well. It has been going on for a few weeks and is now interfering with eating. Give these only if asked specifically: NO weight loss, NO non-healing mouth ulcer, NO lump in the neck or cheek, NO blurred vision or jaw claudication, NO rash or blisters, NO headache waking you from sleep, NO nasal discharge or fever, NO clicking of the jaw. You smoke 10 cigarettes a day. Ideas: you fear it is 'a nerve problem' or cancer. Concerns: you cannot eat properly. Expectations: you want relief and to know the cause. Wince and briefly pause as if a stab occurs when you touch your cheek.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural clinic. A 58-year-old presents with unilateral facial pain. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, state the examination you would perform, and explain your most likely diagnosis and key differentials to the patient in plain language. No haemodynamic-stability screen is required for facial pain. You do not need to give full management.
examiner_instructions: Facial pain is a history-taking station requiring a broad, well-structured differential. Award marks for a structured pain history (SIQORAA, using a 0-10 scale where 0 = no pain) that captures the classic trigeminal neuralgia pattern (paroxysmal, electric-shock, strictly unilateral, triggered by facial movement/wind). Critically, reward RED-FLAG screening: oropharyngeal/salivary-gland cancer (non-healing ulcer, neck lump, weight loss, smoking pack-years), brain tumour compressing the trigeminal nerve (headache, focal deficit), and temporal arteritis in patients over 50 (temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change, PMR). Expected diagnosis: trigeminal neuralgia (normal examination does not exclude it). If asked, examination is normal. Candidate should note MRI to exclude secondary causes and that first-line treatment is carbamazepine. Mark communication for empathy and a plain-language nerve explanation.

criteria: Structured SIQORAA pain history using a 0-10 scale capturing paroxysmal electric-shock unilateral pain
Identifies triggers (chewing, talking, touch, wind) characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia
Red-flag screen for oral/oropharyngeal/salivary-gland cancer (non-healing ulcer, neck lump, weight loss, smoking)
Screens brain tumour/raised ICP and temporal arteritis in a patient over 50
States relevant examination: cranial nerves (esp. V), ENT/oral, lymph nodes, TMJ, temporal artery, eyes
States trigeminal neuralgia as most likely with justification
Recognises a normal examination does not exclude trigeminal neuralgia
Gives sensible differentials (oral cancer, TMJ dysfunction, sinusitis, dental, shingles, temporal arteritis, glaucoma, facial migraine)
Notes MRI to exclude secondary causes (tumour, MS, vascular loop compressing the nerve)
States carbamazepine as first-line treatment with safety awareness
Identifies red-flag pathways (urgent referral for non-healing ulcer; high-dose steroid for temporal arteritis)
Empathy and offers analgesia if the patient shows pain cues
Plain-language explanation of the trigeminal nerve mechanism

red_flags: Persistent painless non-healing mouth ulcer or oral/neck mass in a smoker - oral/oropharyngeal cancer requiring urgent ENT/maxillofacial referral for biopsy
Temporal arteritis in a patient over 50 - temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change - urgent ESR/CRP and immediate high-dose prednisolone to prevent blindness
Brain tumour / space-occupying lesion compressing the trigeminal nerve - focal deficit, headache, requires MRI
Acute angle-closure glaucoma (painful red eye, haloes, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil) - same-day ophthalmology; and herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign
australian_guidelines: eTG: first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia is carbamazepine, with baseline FBC, LFTs and sodium, counselling on hyponatraemia and rash, and HLA-B*15:02 screening in patients of relevant Asian ancestry given SJS/TEN risk

eTG giant cell (temporal) arteritis: start immediate high-dose prednisolone in a patient over 50 with suggestive features and do not wait for temporal artery biopsy, to prevent irreversible visual loss

eTG herpes zoster: oral antiviral (valaciclovir 1 g tds or famciclovir 500 mg tds for 7 days) ideally within 72 hours of rash onset; V1/ophthalmic involvement or Hutchinson sign mandates same-day ophthalmology review
RACGP oral-cancer referral: a painless non-healing ulcer or oral mass persisting beyond 3 weeks, especially in a smoker, warrants urgent ENT/maxillofacial referral for biopsy
learning_objectives: Recognise the classic paroxysmal, trigger-provoked pattern of trigeminal neuralgia
Systematically screen the red-flag mimics of facial pain (oral cancer, temporal arteritis, brain tumour)
Understand that a normal examination does not exclude trigeminal neuralgia and that MRI excludes secondary causes
Know first-line carbamazepine therapy and its Australian safety considerations
key_points: Trigeminal neuralgia is a fraction-of-a-second electric-shock stab, strictly unilateral, triggered by facial movement or wind, with a normal examination
A painless, non-healing oral ulcer in a smoker is oral cancer until proven otherwise - never skip the mouth and neck examination
Always consider temporal arteritis in facial/head pain over 50 and treat with steroids before biopsy to save vision
Use the 0-10 pain scale where 0 = no pain to allow a genuine zero response

citations.claim: The facial-pain differential (trigeminal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, sinusitis, dental abscess, TMJ dysfunction, herpes zoster, parotid tumour, migraine, nasopharyngeal carcinoma) matches the standard causes of facial pain, distinguished from headache.
MRI is used to exclude a brain tumour compressing the trigeminal nerve; unilateral neurological symptoms warrant MRI to exclude an intracranial cause.
Trigeminal sensory testing is performed over the three facial divisions (frontal/maxillary/mandibular).
citations.source: Oxford Handbook of Emergency Medicine 5th Edition (2020)
